Fairness like that has stopped being a sense and become an audit — you brace for the next transaction instead of letting one occur. Nobody's being cheated. It just costs more than the balance is worth.

What holds without crushing is carrying the whole account without closing your hand around it. Endurance is a body bearing weight, not a fist gripping it. You can hold what's owed you and still leave the ledger alone. Take one entry — something you're owed, something you owe — and carry it an hour without collecting or paying. Keep the shape you already have. When you set it down the amount hasn't changed; your grip has.
2.sheetLine: You're keeping score on exchanges that haven't happened yet.

3.tense: For a long while now, things have been out of proportion around you and you have not been the one to say so.
3.verb: To recalibrate what people owe each other until the proportions come right again
3.place: Where a running balance between people is kept level without any still point
3.ask: Run something you can already do again this evening, alone and slowly — repetition for its own sake, not to fix anything and not to prove anything.
3.core:
Where you are owed, you've been letting it stand. Things tip, and you absorb the tip rather than naming it; what's yours by right goes unclaimed and you carry the difference. That works for a while, then the room starts to feel like it's running on something you don't have. You can see the imbalance. Seeing it is not the part that's missing.

What restores the sense of proportion is repetition, done plain. A skill you already have, run again today, alone, with nobody watching and nothing riding on it — that is how fair dealing gets rebuilt, and it does not go through an argument. The session may feel pointless. Run it anyway. It comes back the way any skill does: small repeats, until you notice yourself asking for what you're owed without bracing first.
3.sheetLine: You can see what isn't fair and you've stopped saying so.

4.tense: The tally runs in you now without your hand on it — small debits, kept current, in a book you never opened.
4.verb: To recalibrate what people owe each other until the proportions come right again
4.place: Where a running balance between people is kept level without any still point
4.ask: When something between you and someone feels off, take your first read of it before you work out why — don't argue that read down afterward.
4.core:
You keep the proportions level between the people close to you — easing one side, holding the other — and if asked you'd say it's not your doing. The tally is current. Somewhere in you a running count is kept, small withdrawals and deposits, and the story you tell has no bookkeeper in it. The count is felt by the people it's about, even when you can't see your own hand in it.

No argument is needed for what arrives before any reasoning does. Before you work out why something between you feels off, take the first read you had of it and give it room — it tends to be accurate, and it usually comes earlier than the explanation. Give the reasons their turn afterward. Naming that first read to yourself is the whole act; nobody else has to hear it for the count to come back into your hands.
4.sheetLine: You keep a tally between people you don't know you're keeping.

1.tense: Fairness moves through you now without the arithmetic, and the pen is in your hand.
1.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
1.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars
1.ask: Name one arrangement between you and another that has run its course. Say it's finished, don't reopen it, and let whatever comes next take shape without your design.
1.core:
Under the surface of a thing, you can see an arrangement has gone out of true before anyone says a word. You don't need to count what each side gave; the sense of what's fair sits quiet in you, and you can act from it without a ledger.

So name one arrangement — a split, a standing turn, a way you've both done it since before either of you could say why — and say it's finished. Don't reopen it. What comes next doesn't have to be designed by you; the space can stay open a while and you can watch what arrives. The exchange runs lighter for the room you make, and nobody has to keep score to feel it.
1.sheetLine: You can see it's out of true before anyone says it.

2.tense: You are running the numbers on a fairness that hasn't happened yet.
2.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
2.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars
2.ask: Choose a debt you've been carrying tallies on. Put the tally where you can see it and add no lines to it, whatever anyone asks you to feel about its size.
2.core:
The pattern under an exchange is what you read, and the reading has turned into tracking. Who gave what, when, how much — the glance you used to take has become a record, and the people in the exchange can feel the record even when it stays in your hands. The fairness didn't go anywhere. The counting is standing in front of it.

Choose a debt you've been carrying tallies on and hold it at the size it actually is. Add no lines. When someone asks you to shrink it or make it bigger, keep it where it sits. The weight stays what it is, and the exchange stops needing a bookkeeper. What you were tracking will hold without the tallying.
2.sheetLine: The pattern got a ledger, and the ledger got you.

3.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed a long time ago.
3.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
3.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars
3.ask: Alone today with a page, put something you are owed and have not asked for onto it. Nothing more than that. Same again tomorrow.
3.core:
What fair would look like is visible to you — clearly enough that you know it isn't what's happening. Where things got set right before, asking came to feel expensive, and asking has gone quiet. You take what comes and call it enough. The sense of what's owed hasn't stopped running in you.

Alone with a page today, put something you're owed and haven't asked for onto it. Don't ask yet. Tomorrow, the same. The practice stays small on purpose. It keeps what you already see in your own hand until asking costs less, and nothing out there has to change this week. The page fills. Your hand gets steadier.
3.sheetLine: You can see what's fair and you've stopped asking.

4.tense: You are weighing something this moment, pen down, and don't know the scale is in your hand.
4.verb: to recalibrate what has gone out of proportion until it comes level
4.place: where the pattern underneath a thing shows, stripped of its particulars
4.ask: The situation that's been nagging you — put your first read of it onto paper in a line, before you argue with yourself over it. One line. Then go about the day.
4.core:
Something in an exchange has been running through you as a tally — who did what, what it cost, what they still owe. If someone asked, you'd say you weren't keeping score. The score is being kept, in your own hand, and the counting is the part you haven't looked at.

Before you reason about it, put your first read of the nagging situation onto paper. One line, no argument under it. You saw the imbalance before you could explain it; let that line stay and go about your day. The tally gets its edge back as a perception, which is what it was before it turned into arithmetic. The hand and the scale are the same hand.
4.sheetLine: The tally is yours, and the hand writing it is yours.

1.tense: Right now what you give and what comes back sit level without a tally, and you can tell.
1.verb: leveling what's out of proportion until it sits right again
1.place: the spot where something built on a false floor comes down at once
1.ask: One thing here is already over — a habit, an old arrangement, a favor long since returned. Close it with a single plain act: a note, a shelf cleared, a walk that ends it.
1.core:
What was out of proportion has been coming back to level, and it shows in you — who you owe, who owes you — before any numbers get run. That's the point of it. Fairness at this stage isn't careful; it's obvious. You give and something comes back, and neither side keeps a receipt. That ease is real and it's yours.

And something is already finished that hasn't been marked. An ending wants honoring here — small, plain, not the biggest one on the list — so the next thing has room to arrive. Close the one that's over, once. Then it stays closed, and the space it leaves is easy to spot. The balance you're holding now is what feeds this; the ending is just what makes room for what's next.
1.sheetLine: It's level, and one thing still wants its ending.

2.tense: You're braced for who'll owe you after the next thing falls, writing the ledger before it lands.
2.verb: leveling what's out of proportion until it sits right again
2.place: the spot where something built on a false floor comes down at once
2.ask: Keep your own terms for a week without renegotiating — the same yes, the same no, the same amount you give — and let nobody argue you into a smaller shape.
2.core:
You can see the thing coming that won't hold, and instead of letting it come, you're doing the math in advance: who owes what when it lands, whose share was short last time. Fairness has turned into bookkeeping. People you care about are starting to read as line items on a sheet written for a week that hasn't happened, and carrying that sheet weighs more than the week itself will.

What steadies this is endurance, not correction. Stay your shape — the terms you actually keep, the amount you actually give — without gripping them and without being talked smaller. Stand in the week's weight without deciding the future inside it. When the tally quiets, the fairness runs itself again, and you'll still have your terms.
2.sheetLine: You're already tallying a week that hasn't happened.

3.tense: You stood at a door where claiming turned against you, and you're still standing there after it closed.
3.verb: leveling what's out of proportion until it sits right again
3.place: the spot where something built on a false floor comes down at once
3.ask: Once a day this week, do the smallest practice you keep — alone, ten minutes at most — and ask nothing of it beyond having done it that day.
3.core:
You can say what's owed to you, plainly, and then let it go unclaimed. Not because you miss the unfairness — you see it fine — but asking still stops short in you, and the moment passes. So you take less, wait longer, let things slide by that shouldn't.

Reaching harder isn't the route. A small practice, done alone and kept, is. That steady light rebuilds the floor under you — the part that knows its own weight without needing proof. One repeat today, another tomorrow if you can. Fairness starts to feel safe in your own hands again, and the asking can wait until it does.
3.sheetLine: You see the unfairness clearly, and you still don't claim.

4.tense: Say nothing's being counted, and a column fills itself in the background anyway.
4.verb: leveling what's out of proportion until it sits right again
4.place: the spot where something built on a false floor comes down at once
4.ask: When something stings, hold off on the verdict — no story, no ruling, no change to the count — and stay there until it's plain what the sting was actually about.
4.core:
You'd say you're at peace with all of them, and mean it. Meanwhile a column of names and old slights you didn't plan to keep keeps itself, quietly, running in the back of the day. It isn't that the denial is false. It's that the count stays out of view, so it can't be set down either.

What changes this is a knowing that arrives before the reasoning does. At the moment something stings, stop short of the verdict and wait — ten minutes of not deciding — until it becomes clear which part of it actually matters. Sit with not knowing instead of filling it. That much is enough for the counting to come back under your hand.
4.sheetLine: You say nothing's being counted. Something is.

1.tense: The scale is here, in your hands, and it is steady now.
1.verb: to weigh what's owed and give it its true weight
1.place: the place where something in you is pulling toward what it wants to become
1.ask: Let one arrangement that has already run its course end, plainly, with no announcement — and clear the room behind it.
1.core:
You're being pulled toward something you actually want, and you're carrying it fairly. The people who gave to get you here have what they gave back, in one form or another, and you know the difference between what's owed and what's not. That's the ground the pull is standing on. It doesn't need checking. It runs.

There's a piece of how things are set up that belongs to an earlier version of you — an arrangement, an understanding, a share of something that was fair once and isn't any more. It's already finished. It's still here because closing it takes a plain act and a minute, and those are the things that wait. Close it, accept what that costs, and clear the room. What you're moving toward doesn't need the old shape in the way.
1.sheetLine: Fairness runs in you, and one thing here is already finished.

2.tense: You are adding up what you will be owed before any of it has happened.
2.verb: to weigh what's owed and give it its true weight
2.place: the place where something in you is pulling toward what it wants to become
2.ask: Pick one person you're moving alongside, and for a day, carry the weight of what's between you without counting it — no tally, no mental note.
2.core:
There's a direction you're steering by, and it's a real one. But on the way there, the tracking is running. Who gave what, who'll owe, what you'll get back — the tally turns over in the back of your mind on the walk over. The people you're with can feel the counting rest on them. Nobody's asking you to be careless. The tally has simply grown louder than the care it was there to guard.

There's a kind of strength that carries what's between two people without gripping it. Try that, on one person, for one day. Not a ledger and not a debt — just hold the weight without adding to it, without calling in what's owed. If something's off, you'll see it without having counted. Then it's one thing to answer, instead of arithmetic running every hour. The light you started with stays lit.
2.sheetLine: The counting is louder than the care.

3.tense: The door that closed still has your hand on it, somewhere, even now.
3.verb: to weigh what's owed and give it its true weight
3.place: the place where something in you is pulling toward what it wants to become
3.ask: Do the small thing you do alone — same version, same length — today, and keep it even if nothing comes of it.
3.core:
You can see where you're trying to get, and you're giving more than you're getting back on the way. That's been true for a while, and you've stopped counting it. In this area, asking for what's yours stays hard. The pull is still there. It's just difficult to trust a direction when you're not sure the ground under you will hold.

There's a practice you do alone — a small steady thing, kept by attention. Do it today, all of it, at whatever length is yours, the same way you did it last time. That's how a light comes back: not by being told it matters, but by being kept. Nothing has to be decided about the request you haven't made yet. The repeating is the whole act, and it's enough for today.
3.sheetLine: You give more than you get, and the practice is the way back.

4.tense: You are keeping a tally you would deny keeping, right now.
4.verb: to weigh what's owed and give it its true weight
4.place: the place where something in you is pulling toward what it wants to become
4.ask: Before you settle the next question of who owes what here, stop, and take what came to you first, before the arguing starts.
4.core:
There's something pulling you toward a light you want, and on the way there, you're weighing. You'd say you weren't — that you're not the type to keep score. But the tally is there: small things not returned, chances you didn't get, moments you noticed and filed away. The counting is happening, and your hand on it is out of sight. The counting isn't the problem. Not seeing your hand on it is.

The fix isn't to stop weighing. It's to see the weighing as something you're doing. The next time who-gave-what comes up, don't reason first. Stop, and take what came to you first, before the case you were about to build. That first sense is usually right, and it's usually smaller than the argument. Let it land, and the scale is back in view.
4.sheetLine: The tally is yours. You didn't know it was your hand.

1.tense: The weighing is steady just now, and no case has to be closed for it to hold.
1.verb: Setting what is out of proportion back into right relation
1.place: Where the road ahead is not yet visible and the next step is
1.ask: Give an old matter a plain, visible end: a box set outside, a note burned, a number entered once and the book shut.
1.core:
Where the road ahead isn't visible yet and the next step is, you can feel what's fair without working the calculation. You give and take in a way that leaves no running total in either mouth, and nobody walks away owing more than simply next.

The next step is small and final: give an old matter a plain end. A box set outside, a note you burn, a number entered once and the book shut. None of it needs explaining. The end isn't a verdict on who was right before — it's where you stop reopening something that already happened. What is over gets to be over, and the free hand that comes back is free.
1.sheetLine: Give an old score a plain end and don't reopen it.

2.tense: The reckoning is being run ahead of time, against a bill that hasn't come due.
2.verb: Setting what is out of proportion back into right relation
2.place: Where the road ahead is not yet visible and the next step is
2.ask: Take what you're owed and carry it, undecided, for an hour. Don't forgive it, don't collect it, don't rule on it.
2.core:
Fairness that flows is being pre-spent. You feel what's right, but you keep the ledger open in your head — who owes, who got more, what evens out. Silence starts to look like being shortchanged before anything has been settled.

Take what you're owed and carry it for an hour without deciding anything. Not forgiven, not collected, not forgotten. It will feel bigger than it is while you hold it; let it stay the size it actually is. You don't have to stop noticing it. You only stop ruling on it. The hour ends, nothing breaks, and the balance that was already there gets its turn.
2.sheetLine: You're holding the bill open before it could be paid.

3.tense: A debt went uncollected, and the asking side of it is standing down.
3.verb: Setting what is out of proportion back into right relation
3.place: Where the road ahead is not yet visible and the next step is
3.ask: Do the plain version of a task you keep planning: the first simple step, today, ahead of any scheme. Badly is allowed.
3.core:
Where things are set right, an imbalance sits visible and untouched. You can name it clearly and still let the asking go. Being treated unfairly stopped being something to move on.

Do the plain version of something you keep planning — the first simple step, done today, ahead of any scheme, badly if it has to be. Not the version where you confront anyone. Just the plain move, repeated. Repeating it is what keeps the light on. It won't argue your case in a room you don't control. It does something quieter: it keeps you from becoming the person who lets it stand. The plain step is enough for a day.
3.sheetLine: One plain step today keeps the light on.

4.tense: The tally is running without an author, and the pen is down.
4.verb: Setting what is out of proportion back into right relation
4.place: Where the road ahead is not yet visible and the next step is
4.ask: Put down the first read you had on some unfairness you keep carrying, before you build the case for it. Leave it unargued.
4.core:
The weighing happens in a room you aren't standing in. Notes get kept on who has and hasn't been fair — in a tone you wouldn't put in a message. You wouldn't call it a tally, and it doesn't need calling anything to be kept.

Put down the first read you had on some unfairness you keep carrying, before the reasons. The first read is usually quieter than the case you'd make for it. You don't have to act on it or defend it. Put it somewhere you can see it once. That's all a first line has to do, and it does more than the second one does.
4.sheetLine: The first thing you saw is the one steering.

1.tense: Right now the scale rests level and you already know which way it tips.
1.verb: weighing what each side is owed and letting the scale rest
1.place: standing in the person you're already becoming
1.ask: Something in your life is finished and still getting another week. Give it a plain closing — a box put away, a message sent, a door walked through once — then leave it closed. No announcement needed.
1.core:
You know when something is done. You don't need a verdict weighed out in your head — the tipping shows itself, and you move with it. Offering more than you get back doesn't scare you, and taking your share doesn't need to be argued for. When you leave a room, both sides of the scale are still where they were.

Here the same clear sense could let what's already over actually end. Something is finished, and you keep handing it another week, the way an unclosed debt keeps drawing interest. Give the ending a plain form, small and done with your hands, and don't revisit it. Nobody needs to hear about it. Fairness has room for finishes; what's owed stops being owed the moment the thing stops being alive.
1.sheetLine: You know what's fair. Some ends still need you to let them close.

2.tense: Soon every person in the room will owe something and the ledger will be running.
2.verb: weighing what each side is owed and letting the scale rest
2.place: standing in the person you're already becoming
2.ask: There's a weight you carry for someone else. Hold your own shape underneath it — no shrinking to fit, no adding, no explaining. Let it sit at full size between you for two minutes, then set it down.
2.core:
You track what each person is owed, down to the small debts. The scale rests less and less because you're already weighing what happens next. Someone's relief is a number you can lose. The accounting restores fairness on paper and keeps your own share out of reach.

What holds under all that is your own measure. Hold your shape under it when somebody asks you to shrink to fit their discomfort. Stay standing beside what you know, without proving it or trading it away piece by piece. Their discomfort will still be there for a minute, and that minute is what carrying it whole costs. The weight was not yours to dissolve; it was only yours to hold.
2.sheetLine: You keep the account. Try keeping your measure instead.

3.tense: The door behind you is shut and you are still standing there waiting.
3.verb: weighing what each side is owed and letting the scale rest
3.place: standing in the person you're already becoming
3.ask: Choose a modest thing you can do by yourself today. Do the same one tomorrow. Continue with it on the days when nothing comes of it. Given time, that steady round becomes how you notice what you're owed.
3.core:
You don't reach for what's owed to you. Something unfair arrives and you take it, of course you do, because naming it makes the room go cold. So the asking stopped a while back, and you stand at the door of an old room even though the room has changed.

What builds the missing strength is one modest practice, kept up alone, day after day. It doesn't argue with anyone or demand anything of anyone. It just repeats, quietly, attention rather than force. Claiming your share comes back slowly, by that route, not by a sudden demand across a table. Do the humble version often enough, and then ask for what's yours.
3.sheetLine: You take what comes. A steady practice can teach you to ask.

4.tense: The pen is down in a room you are still writing in.
4.verb: weighing what each side is owed and letting the scale rest
4.place: standing in the person you're already becoming
4.ask: Before you work out whether something was fair, catch what you registered about it before the reasoning started. Say it once, in your own head, and don't argue it. Then leave the arithmetic be.
4.core:
You are tallying what people owe you and don't know you started. The favor goes unreturned and a quiet count begins, one you didn't agree to keep. Ask about it and you'd deny it, honestly, while the numbers keep moving behind the conversation.

What noticed the imbalance first is older and faster than the counting. Next time it stirs, catch whatever you registered before the reasons arrived, before the sum — say it once, in your own head, and don't argue it down. Nobody else hears. The tally runs while you look elsewhere; you can look at the other thing instead.
4.sheetLine: The count runs while you're elsewhere. You knew before it.

1.tense: You are reading the whole shape clearly enough to catch when one part sits slightly off.
1.verb: calibrating what's out of proportion
1.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it
1.ask: One arrangement here has already finished. Say its name to yourself once, then close it in the plainest way you have — a line on a page, a date taken down. You aren't deciding anything; you're freeing the room it was using.
1.core:
You can step back far enough to see the whole shape of a thing, and from there the proportions are mostly right. When someone oversteps, you catch it. When someone carries more than their part, you catch that too. It doesn't sit heavy, because it isn't a tally running underneath — it's just what you see when you look.

That is what keeps the exchange moving here. What this balance is free to feed next is an ending: something in the arrangement has already finished, and letting it close is what frees the space for whatever comes after. Name the thing that's over, then close it in the simplest way — a line on a page, a date taken down, a quiet word that finishes it.
1.sheetLine: You see the whole shape, so an ending here reads as clear.

2.tense: You will be tallying what each person owes the moment this lands in front of you.
2.verb: calibrating what's out of proportion
2.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it
2.ask: Take the next hour of ordinary contact — the group thread, the meal, the meeting. Carry it without settling a single account in your head. When the urge to add it up arrives, wait until the hour is over before judging whether anything needs fixing.
2.core:
Reading the whole shape is something you do well — you see who did what. What's ahead of you is the moment you'll want to reach for the scale. Something already out of proportion will come up, and the plan forms before it has landed: who's ahead, who's behind, what you'll say to even it.

For the next hour of ordinary contact, hold the shape without weighing it. Keep your own frame under the weight of what you see, and don't decide anything yet. If an imbalance is real, it will still be there later and you'll see it better. If it wasn't real, you've saved yourself the accounting. Holding isn't the same as ignoring — it's finishing the hour before you reach for the scale at all.
2.sheetLine: Catch yourself adding it up and finish the hour first.

3.tense: You have been giving past your share for a long while, and you are still standing at that door.
3.verb: calibrating what's out of proportion
3.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it
3.ask: Seeing the imbalance and saying nothing is familiar ground. Today, keep a practice of your own — fifteen minutes on something you've been meaning to get to — and hold it through the days it feels pointless. Alone, no audience, nobody owed.
3.core:
Stepping back to see the whole shape is something you do well, and what you see is your own side of it running short. You give past what's owed more often than not, because asking has stopped being something you reach for. The taking side isn't empty because you have nothing; it's empty because you stopped asking.

What the exchange needs from you is a practice of your own — the kind kept by attention and nothing else. Pick something you do alone, do it again today, and hold it through the days it feels pointless. Nothing is being demanded and nobody has to see it. Do the plain version first, before any plan for it.
3.sheetLine: You see it uneven and stay quiet — begin there, not with a claim.

4.tense: You are already keeping score in a room you did not know you were writing in.
4.verb: calibrating what's out of proportion
4.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it
4.ask: There's a specific person you've been quietly counting things against, and you'd say there's nothing to it. Before you see them next, notice what you already knew about the score before your reasons arrived. Don't settle it. Just catch that you've been keeping it.
4.core:
The whole shape is right there, and mostly you read it the open way — what's true across the room. Somewhere in it a narrower reading is running without your hand on it. Someone keeps coming up short, and a tally is being kept that you did not sit down to keep. If asked, you'd say you're fine with them. The tally says something else, quietly.

You don't have to confront anyone or settle anything. The next time you're near them, notice what you already knew about the score before the reasons got there. Let that first knowing land without arguing it back. That's the whole act — not deciding what the tally means, only knowing that your hand is the one holding the pen.
4.sheetLine: The tally is real and yours — you didn't know you were keeping it.

1.tense: Right now the scales in you are steady and your hand is already on the pen.
1.verb: Weighing what is fair and letting what's finished finish
1.place: Where something has come together whole enough to be let go, and you are the one who lays it down
1.ask: Name the finished thing — a habit, an arrangement, an old grudge. Say to yourself that it is over, and don't pick it back up.
1.core:
The scales settled without any effort from you. You can tell what's fair before running the numbers, and you give and take without keeping a column for either. What you have built here is close to complete, and you can feel the edge of it — the part where finishing something opens a door instead of closing one.

Something you are still carrying is past its date. Not badly, not dramatically; you've kept it going out of tidiness rather than need. Name it as done — quietly, to yourself — and don't reopen it. The gap it makes can stay empty. Ending is the work here, and you're good at it when you remember it's allowed.
1.sheetLine: You can feel what's fair without doing the arithmetic.

2.tense: The ledger in you will be running the totals while the time you were saving runs out.
2.verb: Weighing what is fair and letting what's finished finish
2.place: Where something has come together whole enough to be let go, and you are the one who lays it down
2.ask: Next time the tally starts, ask for what you want in one plain sentence. No itemised account behind it, and nothing added once it's said.
2.core:
Fairness has turned into bookkeeping. You track who owes what, and the tally keeps running in the background even when you're not trying, so a conversation becomes an exchange rate. Underneath it is the truth this faculty is meant for: right relationship, no calculation needed. The calculation is the symptom.

Stopping the count feels like letting yourself be shortchanged, and it isn't. The next time the figures start, right there, say the plain ask instead — one sentence, no account of past debts attached. That's holding your ground without pinning anyone to a ledger. You'll know it worked if you can't remember, by evening, which column the day went in. If you can, you're still adding.
2.sheetLine: The tally keeps running while you're not looking.

3.tense: You stood at a door that is behind you now and you are still standing at it.
3.verb: Weighing what is fair and letting what's finished finish
3.place: Where something has come together whole enough to be let go, and you are the one who lays it down
3.ask: Once a day, pick up whatever you're quietly good at and do it five minutes, alone, with nobody watching. Keep a private mark that it happened.
3.core:
Asking for your share went quiet at some point, and now you let things run uneven rather than risk the ask. You give more than you take, and you've stopped noticing you're doing it. The scale still works in you; it's just not getting any readings to work from.

What feeds this is not a confrontation. It's a small practice kept privately, where you are the only one doing the comparing. Five minutes of something you do without thinking, once a day, marked somewhere nobody else sees. Begin with the plain version, not the improved one. After a week of marks, you'll know something about your own steadiness, and it will be yours before anyone else's. That's the order it comes back in.
3.sheetLine: You let things run uneven rather than risk the asking.

4.tense: The pen is down and the room is being written in without your knowing it.
4.verb: Weighing what is fair and letting what's finished finish
4.place: Where something has come together whole enough to be let go, and you are the one who lays it down
4.ask: When a read on someone arrives, catch the first plain thing you noticed before you explain it away. Keep it somewhere you can look back at.
4.core:
There's a tally running that you didn't open. You carry an old wrong without having decided to, and the sum shows up sideways — in a shortened answer, a hesitation before you agree, a favour you don't make. The weighing is real and competent. You just don't count it as yours.

The first read you get about a person is usually the accurate one, and it gets buried under reasons fast. Catch it before the reasons — the plain thing you noticed, kept as it landed. Don't argue with it, don't tidy it. Look back at what you kept. Whatever's been doing the arithmetic on your behalf will be visible there, in your own hand, and then it's finally something you can pick up or put down.
4.sheetLine: You don't tally it on purpose, but it's tallied.
